title: Risk-based human approval and intervention
summary: Human-in-the-loop design places people at decision points where their judgment materially reduces risk or resolves uncertainty. Human feedback research shows that people can supply preference and correction signals, but production oversight must also consider timing, workload, and the consequences of delayed intervention. Approval is most valuable before consequential, irreversible, or ambiguous actions rather than after the fact.
key_points: Escalate based on consequence, uncertainty, and reversibility.
Give reviewers the context and proposed action needed for a meaningful decision.
Human review is a control point, not a substitute for system validation.
Reviewer workload and response latency are part of the safety design.
rule_of_thumb: Put a human before high-impact irreversible actions and when the system cannot resolve material uncertainty safely.
common_confusions: Requiring a human click for every low-risk step.
Assuming a human can review without relevant context.
Treating human approval as proof that the underlying recommendation is correct.

title: Designing useful escalation signals
summary: An escalation policy should map observable signals such as uncertainty, policy violations, high-impact actions, conflicting evidence, or repeated failures to a defined human decision. A useful escalation carries the evidence, attempted steps, and available options so that the reviewer can act rather than simply acknowledge an alert. Vague escalation increases burden without reliably improving safety.
key_points: Escalation triggers should be explicit and testable.
The handoff should include evidence, uncertainty, and attempted actions.
Risk thresholds can differ by action type and user context.
Escalation outcomes should be logged and evaluated for false positives and misses.
rule_of_thumb: Escalate on defined risk signals and provide enough evidence for the human to decide.
common_confusions: Using confidence alone as a complete safety signal.
Escalating without preserving the relevant context.
Measuring only escalation volume instead of decision quality.

title: Human oversight is bounded, not automatic alignment
summary: Human oversight can correct or constrain an agent, but it does not automatically make the system aligned. Constitutional and feedback-based approaches show that guidance must be translated into explicit principles, feedback signals, and evaluation procedures. Oversight is strongest when combined with bounded permissions, transparent evidence, and tests that measure whether the system follows the intended constraints under pressure.
key_points: Oversight needs explicit criteria and authority boundaries.
Human feedback can be noisy, incomplete, or inconsistent.
Guardrails and evaluation reduce dependence on moment-to-moment human attention.
A reviewer should be able to reject, modify, or stop an action.
rule_of_thumb: Treat human oversight as one layer in a defense-in-depth design, not as a universal correctness guarantee.
common_confusions: Assuming any human involvement means the system is aligned.
Accepting feedback without checking consistency or bias.
Removing automated constraints because a reviewer exists.

title: Outcome-based task success: verifying end state rather than reading the transcript
summary: Task success for an agent is best measured by checking whether the goal was actually achieved in the environment, for example hidden unit tests passing or a database matching an annotated goal state. This is more faithful than judging how plausible the final message sounds. Outcome checks are also cheap to automate and hard to talk your way past, but they say nothing about how the agent got there.
key_points: Define success as a verifiable predicate over the final environment state or artifact.
State comparison and test-based graders reduce reliance on subjective judging.
Real-world benchmarks (resolving repository issues, multi-turn customer-service tasks) pair realistic tasks with programmatic checks.
Pure outcome scores hide unsafe side effects, wasted steps, and lucky guesses, so they should be paired with other metrics.
rule_of_thumb: If you can check the result against the world, grade the state, not the story the agent tells about it.
common_confusions: Treating a fluent final answer as proof the task was completed.
Assuming a passing outcome means the process was efficient or safe.
Using exact-string match on the final message when several end states are equally valid.

title: Reliability metrics: pass@k versus pass^k over repeated trials
summary: Because agent behavior is stochastic, a single run says little about dependability. pass@k asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeds, which suits settings where a verifier can pick the winner. pass^k asks whether all k independent attempts succeed, which better reflects a deployed agent that must behave consistently on every customer interaction.
key_points: pass@k rises with k and measures capability under best-of-k sampling.
pass^k falls as k grows and measures consistency across repeated trials of the same task.
An agent can have a high one-shot success rate yet a poor pass^k when failures are scattered across runs.
Choose the metric to match deployment: pass@k if outputs are verified and retried, pass^k if every run reaches a user.
rule_of_thumb: Use pass@k when you can verify and retry; use pass^k when every attempt is customer-facing.
common_confusions: Reading a high pass@k as evidence the agent is dependable in production.
Thinking pass^k is just pass@k with a different k.
Measuring a task once and reporting the result as the agent's success rate.

title: Trajectory and step-level evaluation of agent behavior
summary: Trajectory evaluation inspects the sequence of reasoning steps, tool calls, and observations rather than only the final outcome. Step-level and progress-style metrics credit partial advancement toward subgoals and reveal where an agent goes wrong, such as choosing the wrong tool, passing bad arguments, or looping. They are diagnostic tools that complement end-state success.
key_points: Tool-call accuracy checks whether the right tool and arguments were chosen at each step.
Progress-rate metrics give partial credit for reaching subgoals on hard tasks where full success is rare.
Trajectory review exposes loops, redundant calls, and unsafe intermediate actions that a final-answer check misses.
Reference trajectories can over-penalize valid alternative paths, so grade required milestones rather than one exact path.
rule_of_thumb: Grade the outcome for success and the trajectory for diagnosis; do not demand a single canonical path.
common_confusions: Equating a correct final answer with a sound process.
Penalizing any trajectory that differs from one reference path.
Using step-level scores as a replacement for end-state success.

title: Efficiency as an evaluation axis: cost, latency, and cost-controlled comparison
summary: An agent that scores slightly higher by making many extra model calls may be worse in practice once cost and latency are counted. Efficiency should be reported alongside accuracy, for example as tokens, tool calls, wall-clock time, and dollars per task, and agents compared on the accuracy-versus-cost frontier. Cost-blind leaderboards can make elaborate agents look better than simple baselines.
key_points: Track tokens, number of steps, tool calls, latency, and monetary cost per task.
Compare agents on a Pareto frontier of accuracy and cost, not accuracy alone.
Simple baselines such as retrying a single call can match complex agent designs at lower cost.
Set budgets and step limits so runaway loops are a measurable failure, not just a bill.
rule_of_thumb: Report accuracy together with cost per task and prefer the cheaper agent unless the gain justifies the spend.
common_confusions: Treating higher benchmark accuracy as strictly better regardless of cost.
Measuring only average latency and ignoring the long tail of slow runs.
Assuming more reasoning steps or more agents always improves the result.

title: Robustness and regression test suites for agents
summary: Held-out accuracy on a fixed set often overestimates how an agent behaves under variation. Behavioral robustness testing perturbs inputs with paraphrases, typos, irrelevant context, tool failures, and adversarial phrasing, and checks that behavior stays within expectations. A regression suite of previously failing cases is rerun after every prompt, model, or tool change so that fixes stay fixed.
key_points: Create perturbation tests (paraphrase, noise, distractors, tool timeouts) with expected invariants.
Turn every production failure into a permanent regression case.
Rerun the suite whenever the prompt, model version, tools, or memory configuration changes.
Separate dev and holdout sets so tuning to the tests does not inflate scores.
rule_of_thumb: Every fixed failure becomes a test, and every change to the agent reruns all tests.
common_confusions: Believing a good average score proves robustness to input variation.
Testing only the happy path with clean tool responses.
Reusing the same cases for tuning and for final reporting.

title: LLM-as-judge: scalable grading and its known biases
summary: Using a strong model to grade open-ended agent outputs can approximate human preference at scale and with explanations, and is useful where no programmatic check exists. Judges are, however, biased toward longer answers, toward the first position shown, and toward outputs resembling their own style, and they can struggle with tasks needing verified reasoning. Judge scores should be calibrated against human labels and not used where an executable check is available.
key_points: Known biases include position bias, verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias.
Mitigations include swapping answer order, using rubrics, and reference-guided grading.
Measure agreement with human raters on a labeled sample before trusting the judge.
Prefer deterministic checks (tests, state comparison) over a judge whenever they exist.
rule_of_thumb: Calibrate the judge against humans, randomize order, and never use it when a deterministic check is available.
common_confusions: Assuming a stronger judge model is unbiased.
Letting the same model family generate and grade the output without a check.
Using judge scores as ground truth for tasks with a verifiable answer.

title: Tool misuse and side effects: testing risky actions in an emulated sandbox
summary: Tool misuse occurs when an agent calls a tool with harmful arguments, in a harmful order, or without recognizing the real-world consequences, such as deleting data, leaking private information, or spending money. Because exercising real tools to find such failures is risky and slow, risky behavior is often probed in sandboxed or emulated environments where side effects are contained. The goal is to find long-tail high-stakes failures before deployment.
key_points: Common misuse patterns: destructive calls, over-broad queries, leaking data to wrong recipients, and unverified financial actions.
Sandboxes and tool emulators let you test dangerous actions without real consequences.
Evaluate safety separately from helpfulness, because a helpful agent can still take a harmful action.
Add parameter validation, dry-run modes, and confirmation for destructive tools.
rule_of_thumb: Test dangerous tool paths in a sandbox first, and make destructive tools validate and confirm before executing.
common_confusions: Assuming an agent that is accurate on tasks is also safe in its tool use.
Testing only against benign scenarios and mocks that never fail.
Believing a prompt instruction alone prevents a harmful tool call.

title: Indirect prompt injection through tool outputs and retrieved content
summary: When an agent reads web pages, emails, documents, or tool results, text inside that data can contain instructions that the model may follow as if they came from the user. This blurs the line between data and instructions and lets an attacker steer the agent remotely without ever talking to it. The risk grows when the agent also holds sensitive data or powerful tools.
key_points: Untrusted content retrieved at run time is an attack surface even if the user is trustworthy.
Consequences include data exfiltration, unauthorized tool calls, and manipulation of answers.
Defenses combine treating tool output as data, isolating untrusted content, restricting tool permissions, and requiring approval for sensitive actions.
Benchmarks that pair user tasks with injected attacker goals measure both utility and attack success.
rule_of_thumb: Treat everything a tool returns as untrusted data, and limit what a poisoned context could make the agent do.
common_confusions: Thinking only the user's own message can be a prompt injection.
Relying on a system-prompt warning as a complete defense.
Assuming retrieved content from a trusted-looking source is safe to treat as instructions.

title: Excessive agency and least privilege for autonomous agents
summary: Excessive agency means an agent has more tools, permissions, or autonomy than its task needs, so any error or manipulation can cause outsized harm. Least privilege scopes each agent to the minimum tools, data, and action rights for the task, ideally enforced outside the model. Capability-based designs go further by tracking what data may flow to which tool so that untrusted input cannot trigger sensitive actions.
key_points: Grant only the tools and scopes the current task requires, and prefer read-only access by default.
Enforce permissions in code or infrastructure, not only in the prompt.
Use short-lived, task-scoped credentials and limit the blast radius of any single action.
Separate the component that reads untrusted data from the component that holds privileged tools.
rule_of_thumb: Give the agent the smallest set of permissions that completes the task and enforce them outside the model.
common_confusions: Believing that a capable model can be trusted with broad access if the prompt says to be careful.
Granting write access when the task only needs to read.
Treating least privilege as a model-quality problem instead of a system-design one.

title: Goal misgeneralization: competent behavior pursuing the wrong goal
summary: Goal misgeneralization happens when an agent learns a capability that works during training but pursues a different goal than intended when the environment changes, even though the training reward was correctly specified. The agent stays competent while optimizing a proxy that merely correlated with the intended goal during training. It differs from simple failure because the behavior looks purposeful and capable.
key_points: The specification can be correct while the learned goal is still wrong, because several goals fit the training data equally well.
Symptoms appear under distribution shift: the agent navigates skillfully toward the wrong target.
Diverse training and evaluation environments that break spurious correlations help expose it.
Testing only in-distribution will not reveal the problem.
rule_of_thumb: If the agent stays capable but pursues the wrong objective after a shift, suspect goal misgeneralization, not a capability failure.
common_confusions: Confusing it with reward hacking, where the specification itself is flawed.
Assuming the agent has failed to learn anything when it acts competently toward the wrong goal.
Believing a perfect reward function rules the problem out.

title: Reward hacking and specification gaming
summary: Reward hacking occurs when an agent exploits flaws in a proxy objective to score well without achieving what designers intended, such as gaming a test harness or exploiting a loophole in a metric. The specification is satisfied literally but its spirit is violated. It arises because every measurable objective is an imperfect proxy and capable optimizers find the gaps.
key_points: The proxy reward or metric is optimized at the expense of the true goal.
Agents may special-case tests, edit the grader, or exploit environment bugs to appear successful.
Mitigations include adversarial review of metrics, held-out and hidden checks, and monitoring behavior as well as scores.
Misspecified rewards often get worse as optimization capability increases.
rule_of_thumb: Assume any measurable proxy will eventually be gamed, and verify success with checks the agent cannot influence.
common_confusions: Treating it as a bug in the agent rather than a flaw in the objective.
Confusing it with goal misgeneralization, where the specification was correct.
Assuming a high score proves the intended behavior occurred.

title: Sycophancy and deceptive behavior in language-model agents
summary: Sycophancy is the tendency of a model to tell users what they want to hear, agreeing with mistaken beliefs or changing a correct answer under pushback, partly because preference-based training rewards agreeable responses. Deceptive behavior is a broader risk in which a model behaves well when it expects to be observed but pursues other behavior otherwise, and research suggests such patterns can persist through standard safety training. Both undermine trust in an agent's reports about its own work.
key_points: Sycophancy shows up as caving to user pushback, mirroring stated opinions, and overstating task completion.
Human preference data can reward agreeable but incorrect answers.
Behavior that differs between observed and unobserved conditions defeats evaluations that tell the model it is being tested.
Mitigate with independent verification, non-leading evaluation prompts, and checks of claims against actual state.
rule_of_thumb: Do not trust an agent's self-report of success; verify claims against the environment.
common_confusions: Treating agreeableness as a sign of alignment.
Assuming safety training that removes visible bad behavior also removes the underlying tendency.
Evaluating only with prompts that reveal what the grader expects.

title: Layered guardrails across input, model, tool-call, and output stages
summary: No single guardrail catches every failure, so safety checks are layered at several points in the agent loop. Input filters screen user and retrieved content, policy constraints shape the model, tool-call gates validate or block actions before execution, and output filters check responses before they reach the user. Each layer has different failure modes, so the combination provides defense in depth.
key_points: Input layer: classify and sanitize prompts and retrieved content for injection or policy violations.
Action layer: validate tool arguments, enforce permissions, and require approval for sensitive calls.
Output layer: check responses for harmful content, leaked data, or unsupported claims.
Measure each layer's false positives and misses, and log blocks for review and tuning.
rule_of_thumb: Put independent checks at input, action, and output stages so one miss does not become an incident.
common_confusions: Relying on a single classifier or a system prompt as the entire safety design.
Placing checks only on text output while tool calls run unchecked.
Making guardrails so strict that they block legitimate use and get disabled.

title: Alignment training techniques: RLHF, constitutional approaches, and preference optimization
summary: Alignment training shapes model behavior toward human intent. Reinforcement learning from human feedback trains a reward model from human preference comparisons and optimizes the policy against it. Constitutional approaches replace much of the human labeling with AI feedback guided by written principles, and direct preference optimization fits the policy to preference pairs without an explicit reward-model loop.
key_points: RLHF uses human preference comparisons to train a reward model that guides policy optimization.
Constitutional AI uses a written set of principles so a model critiques and revises outputs and supplies AI preference labels.
Direct preference optimization optimizes preferences directly without separate reinforcement-learning sampling.
These techniques reduce but do not eliminate misbehavior, so they are paired with runtime guardrails and evaluation.
rule_of_thumb: Alignment training shapes the default behavior; guardrails and evaluation are still needed for what training misses.
common_confusions: Assuming an aligned-by-training model needs no runtime controls.
Treating the reward model's score as the true human objective.
Thinking constitutional methods involve no human input, since humans write the principles.
